On Friday, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association had urged consumers not to resort to panic buying, as excessive purchases could create market distortions. The same day, senators raised concerns over fuel supply even after Minister of State for Finance and Revenue Bilal Azhar Kayani said that there were no supply issues. PPP’s Sherry Rehman questioned petrol availability for December and Opposition Leader Raja Nasir Abbas warned of a bleak situation amid heightening Middle East tensions. The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On Sept 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Regional trade deficit widens sharply. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s trade deficit with nine neighbouring countries widened by 26.62 per cent to $4.97 billion during the first quarter of 2026-27 compared to $3.93bn in the corresponding period last year. The widening gap reflects a contraction in Pakistan’s exports to regional markets, largely due to reduced shipments to Afghanistan and Bangladesh. Trade with Afghanistan, including exports, has remained suspended since Oct 10, 2025, further weighing on overall export performance. Imports from China rose sharply during the July-September quarter, contributing significantly to the widening imbalance. Consequently, the bilateral deficit with China widened by $858.808 million, accounting for approximately 82.18pc of the increase in the combined deficit with the nine countries. Gap with nine neighbours rises 26.6pc to $4.97bn in July-September Exports to China rose marginally, while exports to Nepal also grew in percentage terms, though the increase remained negligible in dollar value. In contrast, shipments to Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka declined, according to the latest data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan. Exports to nine countries—Afghanistan, China, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, India, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives—fell 6.72pc to $944.24mn in July to September of FY27, down from $1.01 billion in the same period last year. By contrast, imports surged 19.79pc to $5.92bn in 3MFY27 from $4.94bn in the same months of the previous fiscal year. Further analysis showed that imports from China grew 19.76pc to $5.82bn in 3MFY27, up from $4.85bn over the same period last year. Pakistan’s exports to China grew 17.95pc to $663.57m in 3MFY27 from $562.56m in the same months of the preceding fiscal year. Imports from India increased by 68.90pc to $61.74m in 3MFY27 from $36.55m over the last year. Meanwhile, no exports to India were recorded in the first quarter of FY27. Exports to Afghanistan fell 88.34pc to $18.86m in 3MFY27, down from $161.76m last year. Imports stood at $0.25m in 3MFY27, compared with $4.52m in FY26, a decline of 94.40pc. Pakistan’s exports to Bangladesh declined by 2.96pc to $174.77m in 3MFY27 from $180.12m over the last year. Imports dipped 36.11pc to $13.88m in 3MFY27 from $21.73m over the last year. Rate hike divides business community. KARACHI: Foreign investors welcomed the State Bank of Pakistan’s (SBP) 50bps rate hike to 12 per cent on Monday, but the business community called it counterproductive for stabilisation, industrial growth and export competitiveness. M. Abdul Aleem, Secretary General of the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry, acknowledged the SBP’s move, saying it was needed to contain inflationary pressure and safeguard macroeconomic stability amid global energy price risks. However, with large-scale manufacturing growth recovering to 1.9pc in July-August FY26 and private-sector credit expanding 14.1pc year-on-year, it is equally important to sustain the emerging momentum in investment and economic activity, he said. As inflationary pressures are significantly influenced by external energy prices and domestic supply constraints, he emphasised that monetary tightening must be complemented by targeted supply-side reforms, fiscal discipline, competitive energy tariffs, broader tax-base coverage and predictable taxation and regulatory policies. Foreign investors back SBP’s move to curb inflation, while industry says it will hurt exports and growth In contrast, FPCCI President Atif Ikram Sheikh said raising the policy rate to an uncompetitive 12pc would further inflate borrowing costs for manufacturers already grappling with unprecedented high overheads, soaring utility tariffs and liquidity constraints. Instead of curbing inflation — driven largely by supply-side bottlenecks, energy costs and fiscal anomalies rather than excess demand — tight monetary policy has crippled domestic manufacturing, he said, urging the government and the State Bank to recalibrate the framework and bring the policy rate to single digits to make credit affordable for trade, SMEs and large-scale manufacturing. High interest rates also place an unmanageable debt-servicing burden on the exchequer and private borrowers, creating a cycle of fiscal distress and stagnant output, he said, asking the SBP to align rates with regional benchmarks. KCCI President Talat Mahmood warned that the hike would further raise the cost of doing business, discourage private-sector investment and undermine growth. He said Pakistan needs to strengthen its productive capacity, attract investment, generate employment and accelerate export-led growth but the policy rate hike will send the wrong signal to businesses planning to invest and expand. SITE Association of Industry President Abdul Hadi said the move would further aggravate industry problems at a time when factories are operating far below capacity and barely surviving. The business community has long demanded a single-digit policy rate, but industry’s real problems have again been ignored, he said, adding that high rates will not only make fresh funding harder but also increase the burden on existing loans. He said the rate hike would burden manufacturers, forcing formal businesses to shut down or scale back, as costlier borrowing would hit new investment, expansion and production. Korangi Association of Trade & Industry President Sheikh Umer Rehan said the hike could hurt industry, business growth, and recovery, adding that inflation could also be curbed by cutting energy costs, fixing taxation, improving the business climate, and implementing effective industrial policies. Pakistan Textile Exporters Association Chairman Rehan Naseem Bharara said the rate hike would raise working-capital costs, constrain investment and weaken global competitiveness at a time when industry is already grappling with expensive energy and financing. Makkah pact allies move from defence to diplomacy. • Pakistan’s army chief, Saudi defence minister, Turkish spymaster meet top Iranian officials • Pezeshkian backs understanding ‘to strengthen unity among Muslim nations’ • Saudis say visit aimed at supporting Qatari, Pakistani mediation efforts • Halting Houthi attacks, reopening Hormuz among main concerns ISLAMABAD: Iran on Monday expressed support for efforts to promote security and development as President Masoud Pezeshkian met senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the three signatories to the Makkah defence pact, with both sides agreeing to continue dialogue on regional peace and security. “The Islamic Republic of Iran supports any understanding aimed at strengthening the unity and cohesion of Islamic nations,” President Pezeshkian was quoted as saying in an official statement. He added that regional countries could set an example of justice and development by pooling their resources and capabilities. The meeting brought together Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin. Iran was represented by senior officials, including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei. The visiting officials met with Mr Rezaei separately ahead of their meeting with President Pezeshkian. During the preliminary meeting, it was decided that they would “continue their dialogue to bolster cooperation among the four regional nations, including in the areas of regional peace and security.” The talks followed Field Marshal Munir’s visit to Tehran last week, where he had proposed the meeting, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. The first meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries with Tehran reflected the realisation that regional tensions need to be addressed through diplomacy, even as the participating countries strengthen their own defence cooperation. (RIGHT) Iranian National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei, President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during talks between Makkah pact members and Iran in Tehran.—AFP Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Ministry described the visit as part of continuing efforts by the agreement’s members to reduce tensions, promote dialogue and support diplomatic solutions. The visit, it said, was aimed to support the mediation efforts of Qatar and Pakistan. Abdul Aziz Hamad Al-Uwaisheq, assistant secretary-general for political affairs and negotiations at the Gulf Cooperation Council, similarly identified de-escalation, dialogue and support for Pakistan and Qatar led mediation as key objectives of the initiative. A Qatari delegation had immediately preceded the visit by Makkah pact officials to Tehran, suggesting coordination between the diplomatic initiatives. The discussions took place against a backdrop of heightened concern over the escalating conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah rebels against Saudi Arabia, the security of the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran. Moreover, the meeting coincided with Egyptian parliament authorising its president to provide defensive military support to Saudi Arabia in its conflict with Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement. Cairo has, meanwhile, maintained contacts with Iran, the United States and other regional partners in an effort to prevent the conflict from widening. In a way the meeting was also an extension of the R4 initiative, with Cairo conducting its diplomacy with Tehran in parallel and the other three going over to Tehran to see Iranian leaders. Iran has long argued that regional security should be managed by countries in the region rather than outside powers. Monday’s meeting offered Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye an opportunity to convey their concerns directly to Iranian leaders, while exploring whether regional cooperation could help contain the risks of a wider conflict. Media reports said the discussions included the possibility of a regional non-aggression framework, along with the resumption of US-Iran negotiations, halting Ansar Allah attacks, the reopening of Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. Other issues reportedly raised included the consequences of US and Israeli military actions and developments in Palestine and Lebanon. There was no immediate indication that the participants had reached an agreement on these issues after their meeting that lasted about two hours. Mr Rezaei, however, speaking to the media later, said, “a new and positive atmosphere has emerged within the region as reflected in the dialogues held with senior officials from Turkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia.” For Pakistan, the initiative offers a means of maintaining its defence partnership with Saudi Arabia while keeping channels open with neighbouring Iran. Islamabad has also sought to facilitate communication between Washington and Tehran, an effort that would become more difficult if regional hostilities resumed. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces the task of strengthening protection for its territory and critical infrastructure from Houthi attacks and fallout of US/Israel-Iran conflict. Its participation in the talks suggests that closer defence cooperation with Pakistan and Turkiye is not precluding engagement with Tehran. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani posted to Pindi bench after reshuffle at Lahore High Court. ISLAMABAD: Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani has returned to the twin cities following a reshuffle at the Lahore High Court (LHC), according to the court’s duty roster for November and December 2026. He will preside over a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry. Justice Kayani hails from Islamabad, while Islamabad and Rawalpindi are traditionally referred to as the twin cities. He was transferred to the LHC in April this year and assigned to its principal seat in Lahore. Despite being a senior judge of the LHC, he was not assigned to any division bench. According to the new duty roster, three division benches at the LHC’s Rawalpindi registry will comprise Justice Sadaqat Ali Khan and Justice Syed Farhad Ali Shah, who will handle criminal matters; Justice Mirza Viqas Rauf and Justice Muhammad Raza Qureshi, who will handle civil matters; and a special division bench comprising Justice Mirza Viqas Rauf and Justice Syed Farhad Ali Shah. The six single benches at the Rawalpindi registry will be headed by Justices Sadaqat Ali Khan, Mirza Viqas Rauf, Mohsin Akhtar Kayani, Muha­mmad Raza Qureshi, Malik Javid Iqbal Wains and Syed Farhad Ali Shah. The roster will remain in effect from Nov 2 to Dec 24, 2026. Justice Kayani previously served as the senior puisne judge of the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and was expecting to be elevated to chief justice. However, the transfer of Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar from the LHC, along with two other judges from the Sindh and Balochistan high courts, prompted him to challenge the inter-high court transfers. The Supreme Court’s constitutional bench upheld the transfers to the IHC, including that of Justice Dogar, who is now its chief justice. The decision, however, triggered a broader legal battle. Justice Kayani and other senior IHC judges approached the SC to challenge the administrative powers exercised by Chief Justice Dogar. They alleged that the office had been turned into a “monocracy” and that judges could be excluded from the roster at will. Following his own transfer to the LHC, Justice Kayani lost his seniority and was placed 12th on the high court’s seniority list. The new duty roster assigns him only to a single bench at the Rawalpindi registry, despite his previous position as the IHC’s senior puisne judge and his pending challenge to the inter-high court transfers. Average price of gasoline during Trump's term now exceeds Biden's, as midterms loom. Americans have paid more for their gasoline and diesel at the pump on average during President Donald Trump’s second term than they did under his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). Surging fuel prices are a major thorn in Trump’s side as midterm elections loom and the Republican Party looks to defend narrow majorities in both legislative chambers on November 3. The price of a gallon of regular gasoline has averaged $3.472 since Trump took office almost two years ago, edging out the $3.471-per-gallon average for Biden’s term, according to data from the AAA. Russia’s war in Ukraine , now in its fifth year, as well as the US-Israeli war with Iran , almost in its ninth month, have both squeezed global crude and fuel supplies and forced emergency oil releases in the US and Europe. The war in Iran has spilled out across the Middle East, with much of the conflict centered around the Strait of Hormuz , through which around a fifth of global oil and gas supplies flowed before the war broke out in February. “Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically… Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. The seven-day moving average for Middle East oil exports, including Hormuz flows and Gulf of Oman shipments as well as Red Sea shipments, reached 24.6 million barrels per day in the week to October 18, according to Kpler, its highest level since the war broke out in late February, and surpassing pre-war levels. Sticky inflation Sticky inflation makes nominal price comparisons misleading, analysts said, with consumer expectations for inflation over the next year nudged up to 4.7 per cent from 4.6pc in September, a survey showed last week. Twelve-month inflation expectations have surged from 3.4pc in February before the US-Israeli war with Iran started. “Adjusting for inflation puts this into context as the value of the dollar continues to impact prices over the longer run. Americans are still not paying record amounts of their income on filling up their tanks,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, on average fuel prices under Trump surpassing those under Biden. Trump’s approval rating fell to a record low this month as Americans worried about high gasoline prices, according to a Reuters /Ipsos poll published on October 19. Some 31pc of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed. Just 23pc of adults polled nationwide approve of his handling of the economy. Prices for diesel, the fuel that powers the global economy from agriculture and heavy industry to shipping, have also surpassed Biden’s national average under Trump, at $4.343 a gallon compared with $4.078 a gallon. US diesel hit a record high on September 22 at $6.523 a gallon.

Flu cases double at Karachi hospitals in over a week amid seasonal shift. • JPMC, CHK report more cases over past 10 days than first half of month • Experts advise frequent hand washing, avoiding close contact with sick people and staying hydrated KARACHI: The city is seeing a spike in the number of flu cases over the past eight to 10 days, senior health experts shared on Monday, urging people to take precautionary measures to cope with changing weather conditions. “We have been seeing patients with flu-like symptoms for over a month but their numbers have just doubled over the past week, rising from 30 to 40 per day to 70 to 80 now, with the gradual seasonal shift towards winter, especially the drop in night-time temperatures,” said Dr Irfan Siddiqui, heading the emergency department of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC). He said, “At the initial stages [of illness], people generally turn to clinics in their neighbourhoods, and it’s only when the disease takes a serious turn that they report to a hospital’s emergency department”. He added that the large number of cases at one of the city’s key tertiary care hospitals indicated that a far greater number of people are being affected in the city and the number of patients visiting the hospital was just the tip of the iceberg. JPMC, CHK report more cases over past 10 days than first half of month The spike in flu cases, he said, was seasonal and that people with weak immune systems, the elderly and children, were more vulnerable. Another factor contributing to the spike, he pointed out, was the general public’s reluctance to adapt their eating habits to changing weather conditions, which could make them more susceptible to illness. Most flu patients currently reporting to the hospital, he said, were aged between 18 and 32 years and belonged to the labour class. A significant number of them were heavy smokers and drug users. “Patients are generally presenting with severe illness and taking a longer-than-usual time for recovery,” he added. Dr Siddiqui emphasised the need to practise good hygiene and maintain healthy habits. He advised people to wash their hands frequently, stay at home when ill, avoid close contact with sick people, stay hydrated and get adequate sleep. He also advised against consuming cold drinks and water. “Getting a flu shot every year [early fall] is the most effective step to reduce the risk of seasonal flu and potential complications. But the vaccine is costly and available only at private healthcare settings.” As at JPMC, the number of flu patients reporting to Dr Ruth Pfau Civil Hospital Karachi (CHK) has doubled in just over a week. “The cases have jumped from eight-10 [a day] to 30 to 40. This includes people of all age groups, though younger people aged 20-30 are dominant,” said Dr Imran Sarwar, additional medical superintendent and head of the emergency department at CHK. “Perhaps it’s more contagious this time as we are getting three to five patients of the same family,” he said, adding that flu treatment was symptomatic, with only a few complicated cases requiring admission. Why the world still needs World Trade Organisation. The World Trade Organisation has spent much of its recent life being told it is obsolete. In its World Trade Report 2026 launched last month, the Geneva-based body tells us what would happen if the rules are simply allowed to ‘wear away.’ It says the outcome would be quite expensive for the global economy. It models a world that breaks into rival geopolitical blocs and finds global GDP would be 5.1 per cent lower by 2050 than it would otherwise be, with exports dropping by 18.6pc. In a harsher scenario, where multilateral cooperation collapses, GDP falls 6.9pc and exports by nearly 27pc. Set against that, a reinforced system could add about 2.9pc to global output and lift exports by almost 18pc. That is roughly three trillion dollars. The report is the WTO’s flagship study and looks back over 80 years of trade rules. It is also a warning: reform the system or risk a slide into fragmentation. WTO Chief Economist Rob Staiger has told Reuters that the trading system is at a “critical juncture”. The report names four pressures: economic power is spread more widely than when the rules were written; governments intervene in their economies far more; digitalisation and global value chains have changed what trade actually is; and political friction between major powers keeps rising. Weaker WTO means riskier world for trade None of this is new to anyone who follows trade. What the report adds is a price tag, and some uncomfortable detail. About 72pc of global merchandise trade still moves on WTO most-favoured-nation (MFN) terms, meaning without special preferences for particular partners. Four years ago the figure was roughly 80pc. Staiger called the slide a “worrisome trend”, and it is the sort of change that does not announce itself. Nobody declares the end of a rules-based order. Trade simply migrates, one exemption and one bilateral deal at a time, until the exception becomes the norm. The WTO says trade policy uncertainty has reached unprecedented levels as governments reach for tariffs, subsidies, export controls and industrial policy. Regional and sector-specific deals are multiplying in response. Without a strong multilateral framework, such arrangements divert trade towards preferred partners rather than the most efficient producers, and encourage blocs to raise barriers against outsiders. The WTO rules restrain discrimination against non-members and shape how free trade agreements are built. Take that discipline away and the incentive to build walls grows. The Trump factor: Erosion of the trading order in recent years cannot be discussed without naming the biggest single force behind it. The protectionism led by the United States under two non-consecutive Trump administrations has been a decisive rupture with the multilateralism that shaped the economy in the last eight decades. What began in 2018 as retaliation against steel and aluminium imports into the US has hardened into a tariff doctrine, revived and widened in Trump’s second term from 2025. It is wrapped in the language of national security and economic sovereignty. However, the logic is strained. Tariffs on allies’ steel were not a response to a security threat, and blanket duties on nearly everything cannot be defended as one. The language of security has become a licence for unilateralism, and it undermines the assumption on which the WTO rests: integration and reciprocity would discipline the strong as well as the weak. The costs are not hypothetical. Studies by the IMF and the US Federal Reserve in the last few years have documented real income losses, disrupted supply chains and weaker investment from earlier rounds of tariffs. Costs for US consumers and manufacturers who depend on imported components have been substantial. The 2025 programme with its blanket tariffs and punitive duties on Chinese goods and electric vehicles, moves US policy from rules-based liberalism towards transactional nationalism, in which access to the American market is a favour to be bargained for. Even at home, the approach has run into legal limits. In May 2025, the US Court of International Trade ruled that the president had exceeded his authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act when imposing a universal 10pc tariff; the appeals court upheld that decision. The rulings are a reminder that policy built on emergency powers is fragile, and that trading partners are being asked to reorder their economies around measures that may not survive scrutiny. When the largest economy treats the rulebook it helped write as optional, others retaliate. Some hedge by building their own blocs and some conclude the rules were only ever meant for others. The report’s most striking finding is about distribution. Least-developed countries would gain the most from stronger multilateral cooperation, and lose the most from fragmentation. Pakistan has experienced this. Its exporters have had to absorb tariff shocks and renegotiate access. Rules do not guarantee fairness, but they make the terms of competition predictable, and predictability is what small economies cannot afford to lose. WTO director-general Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala struck a more hopeful note at the report’s launch. The system has been repaired and refreshed before, she said, and it can happen again. “Let’s not be fearful,” she said. The report does not argue that the system is working as designed. Its argument is that the alternative to imperfect rules is worse, and that the choice is not between the old order and a better one, but between repair and decline. The bottom line is plain. Trade rules are not an administrative distraction. The choice between renewing them and letting them lapse is worth trillions of dollars, especially for countries with the least say in whether the rules survive. Sudan drone strikes kill 21, cause mass outages in east. Sudan’s warring sides have traded drone strikes that killed 21 people in the western Darfur region and left vast swathes of the country’s east without electricity, medics and witnesses said Tuesday. A drone strike on a market in Nyala, the de facto capital of Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Darfur, killed 21 people and wounded at least 40 others, a medical source and witnesses told AFP . One Nyala resident said a market in the city’s north was struck by a drone on Monday around 8pm (11pm PKT). Another said the market was frequented by young men, particularly RSF fighters. “Twenty-one people were killed in last night’s bombing, and more than 40 others injured,” a medic at Nyala Hospital said, though he was unable to identify how many were RSF fighters. Sudan’s military, at war with the RSF since April 2023 , regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivalling the army-backed internationally recognised government in Khartoum. The RSF has in turn launched repeated strikes targeting Khartoum’s airport , as well as dams and power stations across the country’s east. On Tuesday, “RSF militia drones targeted the Al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting the power supply across large parts of Khartoum and Al-Jazira states,” a source in the national electricity company told AFP on condition of anonymity. The strike comes a day after a coordinated RSF drone attack on six power stations left millions without power in Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref states. Famine risk The war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time. In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally. Since it began, the war has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people. Close to three million people have returned to Khartoum state since it was recaptured by the army last year, but many have struggled to rebuild their lives in a scarred city. Power and water supplies remain unreliable, much of the capital remains unsafe from unexploded bombs, and many struggle to put food on the table in a collapsed economy. On Monday, 30 countries including the United States, France and the United Kingdom warned that urgent action was needed to prevent famine expanding across the country. Sudan is facing “an alarming deterioration” of food security, they said, citing the war, a currency in freefall, higher fuel prices due to the Middle East war and a drought induced by the El Nino climate phenomenon . Sudan’s foreign ministry on Monday insisted the country’s food security was “reassuring”, in an attempt to “refute claims of famine”. It accused “some countries and organisations” of “politically exploiting the humanitarian situation”. The army has for years denied claims of documented famine and has been accused of blocking access to humanitarian aid.

Israel to give verdict on Netanyahu in pivotal election. A deeply divided Israel headed to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’s Oct 7, 2023 attack , with voters delivering their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s rightward drift. Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of three years of multi-front regional wars, with the trauma of the Oct 7 attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign. The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by a devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank, along with a move towards hard-right religious nationalism. The last opinion polls to be published showed Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, running neck and neck with his main centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot , a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent. “I want change in our country. I want a good democratic centrist government,” Alexandra, 65, told AFP at a Jerusalem polling station, where a few dozen people waited to vote early in the morning. Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with hundreds of thousands of young people due to cast their ballot for the first time. Surveys show they overwhelmingly identify as centre-right or right-wing. Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad to vote in an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country. “This is the most important election because half the country has rejected the basic values on which the state of Israel was created,” 78-year-old voter Noam told AFP , saying the government was threatening the separation of powers and equality for all citizens. Netanyahu, 77, has served as Israel’s prime minister on and off for more than 19 years. The wily political operator focused heavily on his security credentials during his campaign, playing on his relationship with US President Donald Trump and insisting he is the only one who can keep Israelis safe. In the years since October 7, Netanyahu led multiple wars that have seen Israeli forces reduce Gaza to rubble , occupy southern Lebanon and pummel Iran with US help. ‘Not afraid to take action’ Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu “because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons”, praising his support from the US and adding: “He’s a man who’s not afraid to take action.” Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket. Wearing his trademark noose-shaped lapel pin, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir cast his ballot in the West Bank settlement of Kiryat Arba, where his supporters had set up banners and speakers. The opposition has scorned Netanyahu for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages. But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at the premier is his failure to take responsibility for the Oct 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country’s history. Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu’s government has resisted. Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot’s Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left. Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers. Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 per cent of Israel’s population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected. Yousef Jabareen, who heads one of the Arab-majority lists, told AFP he hoped for a high turnout among his community to help topple Netanyahu’s coalition, after voting in the northern town of Umm al Fahm. Most polling stations will close at 10 pm (2000 GMT). Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament. Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

Pakistan reaffirms solidarity with Kashmiris on Black Day, calls for end to rights violations. The country’s top leadership on Tuesday reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for the people of Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) as the country observed Kashmir Black Day to mark the anniversary of the arrival of Indian forces in Srinagar on Oct 27, 1947. In a statement issued on the occasion, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the arrival of Indian forces in Srinagar 79 years ago marked the beginning of a “tragic chapter” in the history of Jammu and Kashmir, which continued to cast a long shadow over the region. He expressed deep concern over the prolonged incarceration of Kashmiri political leaders, activists and human rights defenders. “Pakistan’s position on Jammu and Kashmir remains clear, consistent and principled,” he said, adding that lasting peace and stability in South Asia could not be achieved without a just and peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people. Paying tribute to the sacrifices of the Kashmiri people, PM said countless men, women and children had made immense sacrifices in pursuit of their rights, adding that their memory would always be honoured. He reaffirmed the government and people of Pakistan’s unwavering solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir. According to a statement issued by the Presidency, President Asif Ali Zardari said the people of IIOJK had endured decades of conflict, restrictions and denial of their fundamental rights since Oct 27, 1947. He said, “continuing restrictions on fundamental freedoms, heightened militarisation, arrests and reports of human rights violations remained a matter of serious concern and underscored the need for sustained international attention”. Dar calls for resolution in line with UN resolutions In his message, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the people of IIOJK continued to be deprived of their fundamental rights under Indian occupation, nearly eight decades after Indian forces entered Srinagar. He said the Kashmiri people’s struggle for the right to self-determination, recognised by the United Nations, remained unfinished, adding that Pakistan stood firmly with them in their pursuit of freedom, dignity and the right to determine their own future. Dar added that India’s unilateral measures of Aug 5, 2019, had further aggravated the situation in the disputed territory, intensified the suffering of its people and could not alter the occupied region’s disputed status. He called on the international community to fulfil its responsibilities towards the Kashmiri people, take sustained notice of the human rights situation in IIOJK and urge India to end rights violations and allow them to exercise their right to self-determination. He paid tribute to the sacrifices of the Kashmiri people and reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to extending them political, diplomatic and moral support. Dar said a just, peaceful and lasting resolution of the dispute in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people was essential for peace and stability in South Asia. He added that the dispute could not be resolved through unilateral actions or the use of force. In his message, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said Kashmiris had been waiting for decades for their right to self-determination, as recognised in United Nations resolutions. He said the international community must answer through its actions when Kashmiris would be granted their recognised right to self-determination. Bilawal said the future of Kashmir’s children should be one of freedom, peace and a life free from fear, rather than another prolonged wait to decide their own future. NA resolution urges sustained diplomatic efforts The National Assembly also unanimously passed a resolution, reaffirming Pakistan’s “unwavering moral, political and diplomatic support” for the people of Jammu and Kashmir and their inalienable right to self-determination. The resolution strongly condemned continuing human rights violations in occupied Kashmir, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests and detentions, enforced disappearances, custodial torture and restrictions on fundamental freedoms. The House also expressed concern over the continued incarceration of Kashmiri political leaders and activists and rejected India’s unilateral actions of Aug 5, 2019, aimed at altering the disputed territory’s status and demographic character. In August 2019, India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had revoked occupied Kashmir’s special status by repealing Article 370 of the constitution. The law had limited the power of the Indian parliament to impose laws in the state, apart from matters of defence, foreign affairs and communications. In its resolution, the NA reaffirmed that the final disposition of the dispute must be determined in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council (UNSC) resolutions and the freely expressed will and aspirations of the Kashmiri people, and called for an end to human rights violations and measures aimed at changing the territory’s demographic character. The House further urged the government to sustain diplomatic efforts at the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and other relevant international forums to highlight the Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions. The resolution said that “neither the passage of time, nor repression, nor unilateral actions could extinguish the legitimate aspirations of the Kashmiri people or diminish the international community’s responsibility to work towards a peaceful and just resolution of the Kashmir dispute”.

No pressure from US to cut Russian oil imports, says Indian oil minister. India has faced no pressure from ​the US to reduce its Russian crude ‌imports , oil minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday at an industry event. “I never felt anything,” Puri said when ​asked if there has been pressure to ​cut Russian oil imports. Puri said Middle East oil ⁠supplies have been rising as the region is ​able to ship out more cargoes. He said India ​was getting 0.2 per cent of its oil imports from Russia before the Ukraine war , while imports have surged since the war ​started due to discounts on Russian oil . India’s imports ​of Middle Eastern crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war ‌levels, ⁠while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition from China, ship-tracking data showed. The minister said that the purchase of Russian oil ​is linked ​to discounts ⁠and pricing when compared with other grades. Russian oil imports have been reduced ​as the refiners are buying more Gulf ​oil ⁠sold at a discount, he added. “Whatever people say or do, ultimately it is anchored in their self-interest,” ⁠he ​said. The minister also said India ​is expanding its refining capacity to help meet local demand and ​export commitments.

India orders evacuations in Andhra Pradesh, Odisha as Cyclone Arnab looms. Indian authorities ordered nearly 100,000 people to evacuate homes in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, ahead of a severe cyclone the national weather office expects to make landfall by Wednesday. Neighbouring Nepal and Sri Lanka have also issued weather warnings. Cyclone Arnab is forecast to hit India’s southwestern Andhra Pradesh coast as a “very severe cyclonic storm”, with gusts of up to 150 kilometres (93 miles) per hour on Wednesday morning, the India Meteorological Department said in a bulletin. Torrential rain lashed the coast in the port city of Kakinda as heavy waves crashed on shore. “I’ve never seen anything like this before,” Kotesh Kumar, 35, told AFP , adding the government warned people to stock up on groceries. “There was a cyclone here three years ago, but the water didn’t rise this much.” Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean. The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming . Neighbouring Sri Lanka , meanwhile, closed schools with warnings of torrential rain, with the island’s Department of Meteorology warning storms could trigger flash floods and mudslides. The military has been placed on alert, Colombo’s Disaster Management Centre said. Indian media reported that as many as 50,000 people have been told to move to safe areas in Andhra Pradesh, and 48,000 in Odisha. Women shield themselves under umbrellas during high tide amid rain and gusty winds as Cyclone Arnab approaches, in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India, on October 27, 2026. — Reuters ‘Damage’ Nepal’s disaster authority issued a warning on Tuesday, saying that as the storm travels inland towards the Himalayas — likely overnight Thursday — it will bring heavy rainfall as well as “a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches”. It called on tourists to avoid travelling to high mountain areas and advised those already there to remain in safe locations. Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic August 26 flood sparked by a glacial mountain collapse, which swept away more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing. India’s weather bureau said it expects the cyclone to result in “total destruction” of thatched houses and create localised flooding, uprooting of power and communication poles, and “widespread damage” to standing crops. In Kakinada, police barricaded roads leading to the sea. Andhra Pradesh State Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu ordered the storm to be “constantly monitored and advance precautions taken”, his office said in a statement on Monday. “Adequate shelters and evacuation arrangements have been made,” New Delhi’s Cabinet Secretariat said in a statement. Docked boats along the harbour amid rain and gusty winds as Cyclone Arnab approaches, in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, India, on October 27, 2026. — Reuters The neighbouring Indian state of Odisha opened 1,735 cyclone shelters and imposed restrictions on movement in landslide-prone zone areas, the state’s information office said. Local media reported that Andhra Pradesh authorities ordered evacuations in key, low-lying areas and shut “all educational institutions” in some districts from Tuesday until Saturday. Over 4,700 pregnant women residing in potentially dangerous sites were moved to hospitals, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

Indian court orders takedown of documentary on billionaire Gautam Adani, PM Modi. An Indian court has ordered the takedown of an online documentary posted by Hotmail co-founder Sabeer Bhatia accusing Prime ​Minister Narendra Modi and billionaire Gautam Adani of cronyism, after Adani Enterprises sued, calling it defamatory. Adani’s flagship firm, Adani ‌Enterprises, told the high court in the eastern city of Kolkata that the documentary, which garnered millions of views on social media in recent days, was riddled with false content and had prompted inquiries from some investors in the company, whom the court order did not name. The documentary “is not a news report or an ​account of proceedings. It is a dramatised narrative,” the court’s takedown order for YouTube, X and Meta issued late on Monday ​said. Adani Enterprises, Modi’s office and Bhatia did not respond to requests for comment, and neither did the social ⁠media companies. Modi’s opponents have often accused the prime minister of having close ties with Adani, saying the business tycoon has received favourable ​treatment over the years. The Indian government and the Adani group have repeatedly denied those allegations. In its challenge, Adani Enterprises told the court ​that it does not seek to restrain constructive criticism of government policy or of business concentration, but Bhatia had suppressed material facts, according to the court order. Bhatia, who is based in the US, wrote on his X account that the lawsuit demands 500 million rupees ($5.25 million) in damages. In one X post, he wrote: “Truth ​is on my side”. “I believe the documentary has rattled Adani Enterprises Limited and struck a nerve at the highest levels,” he wrote. Bhatia is ​the co-founder of the once-popular email service Hotmail, which he sold to Microsoft in 1997. Order to take down In an interim order in force until January 31, 2027, the ‌court ordered ⁠YouTube, X and Meta’s Instagram to remove several posts of the 36-minute film, “The Friendship Files”. It also restrained Bhatia from disseminating the video. Hearings in the case are likely to resume in January. Ahead of the court challenge, police in the state of Maharashtra, which is led by Modi’s ruling alliance, sent a takedown notice to Bhatia on October 19, saying the content “made serious unsubstantiated allegations”. Modi’s political opponents have repeatedly been sharing the ​documentary, saying it reflected similar ​allegations they had made about the ⁠two men. The film used archival footage to trace the history of the relationship between Modi and Adani, starting in the western state of Gujarat, where both men come from. It raised questions about Adani’s winning ​bid for six airports in 2019 after a government rule change that critics say favoured his enterprise — allegations ​similar to those ⁠levelled by the opposition Congress party. The Adani group has denied such allegations and the government says all regulations were complied with and there is no favouritism. Earlier, regional opposition leader and Modi critic Raj Thackeray shared the documentary on his X account, where it garnered 4.8 million views, but took ⁠it down, ​saying he was doing it at the request of the Mumbai police commissioner. Mahua Moitra, ​another political opponent of Modi and a lawmaker, posted the documentary on October 11 and said it was still online. “I posted this on Oct 11th. It is still ​on my timeline, so do watch it,” she wrote on X on Monday night.

Pakistan, China launch information corridor 'CPIC' to counter misleading narratives, promote cultural exchange. Pakistan and China have launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), with Information Minister Ataullah Tarar saying that the initiative will focus on countering misleading narratives, cultural exchanges and cooperation between think tanks. The corridor was launched at a ceremony in Islamabad, which was televised on Tuesday. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning and Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong attended the launch. In his televised remarks, Tarar expressed his “long-standing“ desire to collaborate with China in the fields of media, information sharing and digital platforms. Hailing Pakistan and China’s bilateral relations, Tarar recalled the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), noting that it had “turned decades of goodwill into steel, concrete and current”. “It lit homes, laid motorways across our provinces and gave Pakistan at Gwadar a gateway to the world.” Tarar said that while the first phase of CPEC connected lands, the next phase will “connect our minds and this information corridor will act as a bridge for connecting the minds of the people of the two countries”. The information minister said the collaboration under the newly launched corridor will stand on four pillars — media, business and enterprises, think tanks, and culture/tourism. “First, media. A news exchange working group of 18 Pakistani and Chinese media organisations. From our state broadcasters and private channels to Xinhua, CMG, and People’s Daily now share verified news on our cooperation.” He added that it will also include a dedicated fact-check mechanism to track misleading narratives and counter them with “concrete facts”. The second pillar, which includes businesses and enterprise, Tarar said, will draw on leading Pakistani and Chinese commercial groups. “This pillar has opened its first regional office in Karachi,” Tarar said, adding that under the initiative, a trade portal to track trade, investment, and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) was being built, along with a podcast series about the stories of Chinese entrepreneurs in Pakistan and vice versa. He said the third pillar will involve collaboration between think tanks from the two countries. “Led by the Pakistan-China Institute and joined by our foremost research institutions, this pillar will bring evidence and depth to the bilateral conversation through joint dialogue, research, and publications with Chinese counterparts,” Tarar said. The fourth pillar, which Tarar described as the “heart of the corridor”, will focus on tourism, with work already underway on the Xinjiang-Gilgit-Baltistan tourism corridor, “extending the journeys of Chinese travellers into the valleys of our north”. Tarar also shared that the first cohort of CPEC Youth Ambassadors had been nominated from 13 universities across Pakistan. “Before a community of shared future can be built in steel and stone, it must find its place in the minds of the people,” Tarar said, stressing that the principle was at the core of CPIC. “If CPEC is its body and the shared future, CPIC will be its voice. If CPEC connects our economies, CPIC will connect our understanding. Through it, a student in Lahore will know the China of today, and not the caricatures of yesterday. A family in Chengdu will see Pakistan as it truly is: warm, resilient, and full of potential.” He added that the corridor will counter “falsehoods with fact, isolation with exchange, and suspicion with trust,” lauding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s vision. “President Xi gave us the vision of a shared future, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has given Pakistan the means to reach it,” Tarar said. For PM Shehbaz, Tarar said the digital revolution was about people and “above all Pakistan’s young people”. “More than 68 per cent of our nation is under 30 in their hands. A laptop is a passport and a smartphone is a marketplace. Through their talent, Pakistan is taking its place in the global digital economy.” Tarar further stated that CPIC was at its core a “digital corridor”. “Its news exchanges, fact-check mechanisms, trade portals, podcasts, social media channels, and youth ambassadors are tools of a digital age put to work for an old and trusted friendship. And here too, Pakistan walks with China,” Tarar said. The information minister, in his address, also invited Chinese media houses, think tanks, universities, enterprises, and youth ambassadors to join each pillar of CPIC. Concluding his address, Tarar said that while the Karakoram Highway was carved through the mountains, today Pakistan and China were building a “different highway [..] it is not made of rocks, but it is made of truth, and it will be carried not on trucks, but on voices. Meanwhile, China’s Ning also addressed the ceremony, noting that China and Pakistan continue to face misinformation and fake news, according to state broadcaster Pakistan TV. Ning stressed the need for the CPIC, saying that its four pillars can play a key role in highlighting bilateral cooperation. Pakistan and China share a longstanding strategic partnership rooted in mutual trust, economic cooperation and regional connectivity. Over the decades, ties have expanded across different sectors — including trade, energy, defence and infrastructure — with the CPEC symbolising a shared vision for development. A day earlier, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Ambassador Zaidong to review progress on CPEC. During the meeting in Islamabad, Dar praised the ongoing expansion of the “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership” between the two nations. Discussions focused on advancing trade, investment, regional connectivity, agricultural modernisation and people-to-people exchanges.

At UNGA debate, Pakistan warns against adding more permanent members to Security Council, extending veto privileges. Pakistan has warned that adding more permanent members to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and extending veto privileges would “deepen existing inequalities, perpetuate historical advantages and increase the risk of Council paralysis”. The counsellor at the Pakistan Mission at UN, Gul Qaiser Sarwani, presented these views at the UN General Assembly during a debate on the use of the veto. He said Pakistan called for “comprehensive, democratic and equitable reform of the UN Security Council” and stressed that the misuse of veto power undermined UNSC’s effectiveness, weakened the credibility of the UN and perpetuated inequalities within the international system. “Strategic rivalries and narrow interests among the Council’s permanent members had repeatedly impeded collective action on international peace and security,” he said, emphasising the “unique legitimacy” of the UNGA, whose universal membership and democratic decision-making enabled it to respond when the UNSC unable to act, including due to the exercise of the veto. The Pakistani delegate opposed the creation of any new permanent seats in an expanded Security Council. On proposals to regulate the use of the veto, he said Pakistan favoured its abolition or, at a minimum, severe restrictions on its use. He emphasised that the veto must not be expanded and reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for General Assembly resolution 76/262, which provides for a UNGA debate following the exercise of a veto to promote greater accountability. Sarwani stressed that any measures to restrain the veto must remain consistent with the UN Charter. He called for a balanced approach combining restrictions on veto use with enhanced representation and a stronger role for elected members of the UNSC, making its decision-making “more democratic and providing an effective check on the exercise of veto power”. The delegate further emphasised that the question of the veto must be addressed alongside the other four interrelated clusters under the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform, as part of a comprehensive reform package. Concluding his remarks, he reiterated “Pakistan’s strong commitment to reform that corrects existing imbalances, strengthens accountability and serves the collective interests of the entire UN membership rather than a select few”. “Reform for all. Privilege for None!” he said. A recent UN report has also warned that the veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council is one of the reasons multilateral mechanisms have been unable to prevent or stop the growing number of state-based conflicts. The resulting paralysis has weakened decision-making processes, prompting the UN secretary general to call for Security Council reforms, including an expansion of its membership to ensure fairer representation, particularly for Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Asia-Pacific region, it says. “All these voices are underrepresented despite bearing much of the burden of peacemaking in an increasingly multipolar world,” the ‘World Social Report 2026’ notes.

Lahore ATC denies police further remand of PTI's Hammad Azhar, sends him on judicial remand. LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Tuesday rejected a police request for further physical remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar in the Jinnah House attack case and sent him to jail on judicial remand. Sarwar Road police had booked several PTI leaders and workers on charges of attacking and vandalising Jinnah House during the May 9, 2023 protests against the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. According to his family , Azhar was arrested on Sept 5. However, police said the next day they were unaware of his arrest, and he was produced before an ATC on Sept 7. His initial 21-day physical remand was extended at least twice . Subsequently, upon the completion of the latest 12-day remand, the PTI leader was presented before ATC Judge Sardar Muhammad Akram Khan on Tuesday. The investigating officer sought further physical remand of the former finance minister, stating that the police wanted to conduct a polygraph test , also known as a lie detector test. However, Azhar’s counsel, Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi, argued that a polygraph test required the suspect’s consent. He argued that according to a Lahore High Court judgment , the procedure was to be conducted during judicial remand. The lawyer said the suspect was also required to make a statement before a magistrate indicating whether he wished to undergo the test. Azhar told the court that he did not want to undergo the test if the law allowed him to refuse it. He said a suspect should not be punished for the prosecution’s alleged lack of knowledge about the legal requirements. After hearing arguments from the prosecution and the defence over the proposed polygraph test, Judge Akram dismissed the police request for further physical remand and sent Azhar to jail under judicial custody. Barrister Niazi hailed the verdict, writing on X that his client’s “50-day physical remand finally ends” and that he was sent to Kot Lakhpat jail. Azhar served as a federal minister for multiple portfolios during the PTI government, including finance, industries and energy . In the aftermath of the May 2023 riots, when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership, he had gone into hiding and reappeared in public a year later, on May 22, 2024. In 2025, he reiterated his decision to step down as the president of the PTI’s Punjab chapter, citing a lack of access to Imran.

JI chief reaches PM House for meeting with prime minister: party. Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman arrived on Tuesday at the Prime Minister’s House for a meeting with the premier, according to the party. The meeting regards the JI’s demand that the government abolish petroleum levies . The Centre and JI had agreed to form committees in early September — when the latter had planned a nationwide strike — to recommend measures to reduce the levy. Rehman was accompanied by a delegation including the party’s Deputy Emir Liaquat Baloch, Deputy Secretary General Syed Farasat Shah, and JI Islamabad Emir Nasrullah Randhawa, a post by the JI’s account on social media said. The JI has been demanding for over two months that the Centre abolish petroleum levies, as fuel prices have skyrocketed due to conflicts in the Middle East since March. Rehman on Monday warned that the party would march to Islamabad in mid-November if the premier did not abolish the petroleum levy. On Aug 16, the JI announced sit-ins in all the provincial capitals of Pakistan against the petroleum levy and had called for a nationwide strike on Sept 3. On Sept 20, the party launched a protest march towards Islamabad, warning that if the government failed to abolish the petroleum levy, the protest could turn into one to oust the government. On Sept 22, the JI emir said his party, whose convoy had reached Multan, was postponing its long march at the request of PM Shehbaz, who had assured the other side of a meeting to discuss the matters. However, in a press release issued last week, the party alleged that the government had made no further contact regarding the planned meeting.

Chromebook scheme. THE government’s plan to distribute 500,000 Chromebooks to students over two years could help narrow Pakistan’s digital divide. The devices, which will come with MiFi internet connectivity, are meant for students handpicked under the scheme. In a country where access to computers and reliable internet still depends heavily on family income and location, that matters. A student who cannot afford a laptop should not be locked out of online learning, digital skills or job opportunities. But the value of the scheme will depend on how it is carried out. The state should publish clear eligibility criteria, ensure that poorer students are not crowded out by those who already have devices, and explain how the refurbished Chromebooks will be procured, tested and distributed. The total cost should also be disclosed, along with safeguards against political influence in selecting recipients and suppliers. There should also be a plan for repairs, replacement and technical support. A device that stops working after a few months, or cannot connect reliably outside major cities, will do little to close the gap it was meant to address. More importantly, access to hardware is only one part of Pakistan’s education problem . A Chromebook cannot compensate for weak teaching, poor literacy, overcrowded classrooms or schools without dependable electricity and internet access. Nor will handing out devices automatically improve learning. Teachers need training to use digital tools well, students need access to useful content, and schools need systems that can blend technology with ordinary classroom instruction. The government should therefore set measurable goals for the scheme: whether students use the devices regularly for learning, whether their digital skills improve, and whether this leads to better educational outcomes. Independent evaluation would help determine if the programme deserves expansion. There is also a case for giving students in remote and low-income areas greater weight, since they stand to benefit most from access they currently lack. Pakistan has launched laptop schemes before; what matters now is whether this one produces more than a distribution ceremony. Technology can widen opportunity, but only when it is tied to good teaching, reliable connectivity and clear educational purpose. Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

At least 1 killed, 6 injured as roof of under-construction building collapses in Multan. LAHORE: At least one individual was killed, while six others were injured on Tuesday when the roof of an under-construction building collapsed near Multan’s Northern Bypass, Rescue 1122 said. In a statement, the rescue service said the roof of an under-construction plaza had collapsed near the National College of Business Administration and Economics on Northern Bypass. The agency said that so far, six injured individuals had been rescued and shifted to Nishtar Hospital, adding that one person was killed in the collapse. Rescue officials launch a search and rescue operation after building collapse in Multan on October 27, 2026. — Photo via Rescue 1122 A rescue operation was underway to rescue trapped individuals, Rescue 1122 said, adding that at least 10 to 15 labourers were working at the site at the time of the incident. Upon receiving the information, Rescue 1122 relief teams were immediately dispatched to the incident site, the statement said. “Rescue 1122 teams reached the incident site within three minutes and initiated the search and rescue operation,” it said. The statement said 10 vehicles were actively engaged in the relief operations. The relief operations include five ambulances, three rescue motorbikes, one rescue vehicle, and one fire vehicle, it added. Rescue officials launch a search and rescue operation after building collapse in Multan on October 27, 2026. — Photo via Rescue 1122 In a statement, a spokesperson for Nishtar Hospital said that six injured were shifted to the hospital, adding that the hospital record showed that another individual was brought dead. As per the records, three injured received head injuries — whose nature and criticality are unknown — while the other three received minor injuries. The spokesperson said doctors and paramedical staff were on high alert in the emergency room, and the best medical facilities were being provided to the injured. Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, often attributed to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials. A teacher and 30 students were killed when a school’s roof collapsed in Peshawar earlier this month. In September, two men died in Pakpattan after the roof of their house collapsed during heavy rain and a windstorm. On June 30, 14 children lost their lives when the roof of a private tuition centre collapsed in Lahore’s Kahna area.

Madushanka’s five-for powers Sri Lanka into tri-series final after Pakistan drubbing. Sri Lanka stormed into the final of the One-day International tri-series after overwhelming Pakistan by eight wickets, chasing a modest target of 111 in just 18.1 overs at the Gaddafi Stadium on Tuesday. Left-arm pacer Dilshan Madushanka delivered a career-best five for 34 to dismantle Pakistan for 110 in 25.3 overs before Kamindu Mendis struck an unbeaten 62 to guide Sri Lanka to 114-2, sealing victory with 31.5 overs to spare. The result confirmed Sri Lanka’s place in Saturday’s final alongside Pakistan, who had already qualified after winning their first three matches. England’s remaining league fixture against Sri Lanka on Thursday consequently became a dead rubber. Pakistan’s batting collapsed against a disciplined Sri Lankan attack after captain Kusal Mendis won the toss and elected to field. The hosts struggled to cope with Madushanka’s short-pitched deliveries and never recovered from losing wickets at regular intervals. Babar Azam top-scored with 29 off 33 balls, including five boundaries, while Hasan Nawaz made 17. Captain Shaheen Shah Afridi contributed 15 off 13 deliveries, striking two sixes in a late attempt to lift the total. Pakistan lost Fakhar Zaman for five in the fourth over when he mistimed a short delivery from Madushanka and was caught at point. Maaz Sadaqat, making his first appearance in the tri-series after being added to the squad a day earlier, managed eight before Asitha Fernando trapped him leg-before with a yorker. Saad Baig fell for five, caught at short cover off Madushanka, while Salman Ali Agha made nine before edging Sahan Arachchige behind. Pakistan were 61-4 when Babar was trapped leg-before by Eshan Malinga for 29, having already lost their two reviews. The collapse gathered pace as Arachchige dismissed Shadab Khan for two and Dunith Wellalage removed Hasan Nawaz, who was caught by Arachchige for 17. Pakistan slumped to 91-8, leaving the lower order with too much to do. Madushanka returned to claim the remaining wickets, dismissing Arafat Minhas for 10 and Haris Rauf for one before ending the innings with Shaheen’s wicket. The Pakistan captain’s brief counterattack included two sixes, but he was caught by Wellalage as Madushanka completed his five-wicket haul. Arachchige took two wickets, while Asitha, Malinga and Wellalage claimed one apiece. Sri Lanka’s reply began aggressively, with Kamindu and Avishka Fernando putting on 50 for the opening wicket in 6.5 overs. Avishka struck two fours in his 17-ball 16 before pulling Shaheen to Fakhar at short midwicket. Kamindu, however, continued to score freely, reaching his half-century off 43 balls. He survived a dropped catch in Shaheen’s opening over and successfully reviewed an lbw decision before going on to finish unbeaten on 62 from 60 deliveries, with eight fours and two sixes. Pakistan briefly found another breakthrough when Kusal, who had struck two boundaries in his six-ball eight, was bowled by Arafat for 8. The dismissal came in unusual fashion, as the ball ricocheted off the batter’s bat and into the stumps. But the hosts could not build on the wicket. Pavan Rathnayake joined Kamindu and remained unbeaten on 23 off 26 balls, striking two fours as the pair guided Sri Lanka home without further loss. Kamindu’s fluent innings ensured the chase remained firmly under control, while Rathnayake finished the contest by driving Maaz’s spin through cover-point for four. Shaheen and Arafat took one wicket each, but Pakistan’s total left their bowlers with little margin for error. Sri Lanka completed a comprehensive victory that capped a strong turnaround in the tournament, with their batters having also impressed in their earlier win over England. For Pakistan, the defeat exposed familiar top-order weaknesses after their dramatic one-wicket victory over England on Sunday. Shadab’s unbeaten century had rescued that match, but this time the batting line-up failed to provide a competitive total. Madushanka’s outstanding spell proved decisive, giving Sri Lanka the momentum to secure qualification and setting up a final against Pakistan on Saturday.
