By 2023, militant attacks had become so regular in Jammu that the government was forced to revive a defunct militia known as the Village Defence Guards, arming and training hundreds of villagers across the region. 71 These militias were first formed in the mid-1990s, at the height of the Kashmiri insurgency, but the government disbanded them when militancy declined. “India revives civil militia after Hindu killings in Kashmir”, AP, 28 February 2023. On 9 June 2024, just hours after Prime Minister Modi was sworn in for a third consecutive term, militants assailed a bus carrying Hindu pilgrims, killing nine and injuring more than 30 in Jammu’s Reasi district. 72 “Terrorist attack at Reasi sets alarm bells ringing in India’s security establishment”, The Diplomat , 20 June 2024. The attack appeared to have been timed to contradict the government’s narrative of a peaceful region open for visitors. 73 Crisis Group noted in 2022 that tourists “could well become targets, particularly if the government continues to insist that robust tourism is a sign of normalcy”. See Praveen Donthi, “ Violence in Kashmir: Why a Spike in Killings Signals Ominous New Trend ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 28 June 2022. Before becoming chief minister, Omar Abdullah also cautioned that by “[linking] tourism with normalcy, [officials] put tourists in danger”. See “Tourist arrivals in Kashmir not an accurate gauge of normalcy: Omar Abdullah”, Business Standard , 20 May 2024. Indian officials, for their part, have blamed the spike in violence in Jammu on Pakistan-based militants sneaking across the border. 74 “Jammu and Kashmir: Surge in attacks brings fear to calmer parts of Himalayan territory”, BBC, 23 July 2024. D. “Foreign Militants” Indian officials say the outfits attacking non-locals in Indian-administered Kashmir (and increasingly in Jammu) are not new, but the same groups that Pakistan has long supported, above all Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, just with new names. According to New Delhi, both groups rebranded themselves to enable Islamabad to evade scrutiny by the Financial Action Task Force over allegations of funding terrorist groups. 75 The Task Force had until October 2022 placed Pakistan on its grey list for failing to curb money laundering and financing of these outfits. “Pakistan is out of FATF ‘grey list’ on terror funding”, The Hindu , 22 October 2022. Furthermore, Indian officials allege, “foreign militants” have assumed increasing responsibilities in these organisations of late. They claim that the militants allegedly infiltrating Jammu are more dangerous than their predecessors, mainly because they seem well trained and the police cannot track them through family connections. “Some of the old tactics are back”, a retired police chief of Jammu and Kashmir observed, referring to the period from the 1990s to the early 2000s, when Jammu was rife with militancy, and Pakistanis made up a sizeable portion of militant ranks “So we also need to revisit the old tactics and learnings on our side”. 76 “Pak control, narrative war, white-collar terror: Ex-DGP of J&K R. S. Swain’s first big interview”, op. cit. Indian officials also claim that these “foreign militants” have sophisticated weapons, and are adept at avoiding detection, particularly by using encrypted Chinese satellite phones (part of the BeiDou network) whose transmissions are difficult to intercept. 77 Militants have been found using weapons such as U.S.-made M4 assault rifles. Crisis Group interviews, security officials, Jammu and Srinagar, 2025. See also “US arms left in Afghanistan are turning up in a different conflict”, NBC News, 30 January 2023; and “Hard-to-crack Chinese devices part of terror toolkit,” The Economic Times , 30 April 2025. If true, it would be a striking evolution from the years before 2019, when militants were largely untrained and poorly equipped locals. By the end of 2023, Indian forces say, “foreign militants” had come to outnumber local insurgents. 78 “Security situation improved significantly in J&K in 2023; foreign terrorists our target for 2024, says DGP”, The Hindu , 31 December 2023. After the deadly terror attack in Pahalgam in 2025, New Delhi was quick to hold Pakistan responsible, though it has yet to present any concrete evidence to back its accusations. 79 “A year on, India has failed to substantiate allegations against Pakistan over Pahalgam attack: info minister”, Dawn , 22 May 2026. The government’s determination to pacify Kashmir led to broad anti-terror laws, which locals view as collective punishment, fuelling resentment against the Indian state and proving counterproductive. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi IV. The India-Pakistan Fault Line Kashmir’s conflict is inseparable from the dispute between India and Pakistan, which have already waged two wars (1947-1948 and 1965) over the territory and made several smaller forays into armed conflict. A third war erupted in 1971, after India intervened militarily on behalf of the Bengali struggle for independence in Pakistan’s eastern wing, which led soon thereafter to sovereignty for Bangladesh. 80 From May to July 1999, the sides clashed in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kargil district, with hundreds of soldiers killed. In 2019, they engaged in short-lived air combat following an attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 40 Indian troops. In April 2025, the militant attack on Indian tourists in Pahalgam in southern Kashmir triggered the most serious fighting between the two neighbours in decades, after India blamed Pakistan for the massacre. Four days of hostilities ended with a ceasefire on 10 May. Though New Delhi promised systematic retaliation against Islamabad if further attacks occurred on its soil, it stayed its hand when young Kashmiris carried out a suicide bombing in New Delhi on 10 November 2025. With India continuing to claim that Pakistan uses anti-India jihadist groups to wage a proxy war in Kashmir, another terror attack in the region or elsewhere in India could threaten a fragile ceasefire. A. The Pahalgam Attack and Its Aftermath The 22 April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, which saw militants shoot 26 people at point-blank range at a popular tourist destination in southern Kashmir, was the deadliest attack on civilians in over two decades. Most of the victims were Hindu tourists, whose religion the militants ascertained before gunning them down. 81 The victims also included a local Kashmiri who tried to intervene and an Indian Christian. Praveen Donthi, “Deadly Kashmir Militant Attack Raises Temperature Between India and Pakistan”, Crisis Group Commentary, 25 April 2025. The Indian government immediately blamed Pakistan, alleging that it wanted to “undermine normalcy returning to Jammu and Kashmir”, disrupt the economy and “create a fertile ground for continued cross-border terrorism”. 82 “Transcript of Special Briefing on OPERATION SINDOOR”, Indian Ministry of External Affairs, 7 May 2025. Hours after the attack, New Delhi further downgraded diplomatic ties with Islamabad, shut Indian airspace to Pakistan-registered aircraft, closed the only border crossing and suspended the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty. Islamabad responded in kind. Denying Indian allegations that the Pahalgam assailants had any cross-border connections, Islamabad accused New Delhi of making these charges without evidence, while rejecting Pakistan’s suggestions of an independent international investigation into the attack. 83 On 26 April, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Islamabad was open to participating in any neutral, transparent and credible investigation of the attack. “PM Shehbaz says Pakistan open to credible, transparent probe into Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 26 April 2025. New Delhi regarded Islamabad’s offer as disingenuous, pointing to its record of supporting anti-Indian jihadist proxies. Islamabad insisted in turn that the Modi government’s belligerent rhetoric was intended to whip up nationalist sentiment as it planned a military attack on Pakistan. 84 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, Indian forces detained thousands of Kashmiris, informing the media that the attackers had been locals. 85 “If the photographs didn’t belong to the Pahalgam attackers, what were the actions based on?”, Kashmir Times , 4 July 2025. State forces destroyed the houses of at least six suspected local militants. But the National Investigation Agency eventually listed seven accused, including the Pakistan-based heads of Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and The Resistance Front; it concluded that three Pakistanis had carried out the attack, while two local Kashmiris had provided them with food and shelter. 86 “NIA charges four LeT-TRF terrorists in Pahalgam attack”, The Hindu , 16 December 2025. In July 2025, India claimed to have killed all three of the Pakistanis, though without making the evidence public, and arrested the two Kashmiris allegedly involved. 87 Addressing parliament, Home Minister Amit Shah said security forces had established that the assailants were Pakistanis because they found Pakistani voter cards and chocolates made in Pakistan on the bodies. No further evidence was provided. “Three Pakistani terrorists behind Pahalgam terror attack killed in Operation Mahadev, centre tells Lok Sabha”, The Hindu , 29 July 2025. The terror attack on tourists visiting from throughout India, most of whom were shot dead in front of their families, shocked Kashmiris, who organised spontaneous protests condemning the killings. Many locals were also apprehensive about the backlash they knew was coming. Notwithstanding widespread public condemnation of the massacre, a section of Kashmiri society, according to a leading journalist in the region, viewed it as a consequence of New Delhi’s stranglehold on the region. 88 Crisis Group interview, senior Kashmiri journalist, 2025. Throughout the rest of India, the killings provoked a furore, as well as mounting pressure on the government to retaliate against Pakistan. On 7 May, India launched Operation Sindoor, carrying out cross-border strikes on what it claimed was “terrorist infrastructure” across the border. This first salvo gave rise to a short but fierce exchange of fire, in which the two sides carried out tit-for-tat attacks using weaponised drones and missiles deep inside each other’s territory and across the Line of Control, the informal frontier that separates the Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Jammu and Kashmir. 89 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. After four days of conflict, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the two countries had agreed to a ceasefire, which Indian and Pakistani authorities confirmed. New Delhi said it was the Pakistani military that had requested the truce through a hotline between the directors general of military operations – the only official line of communication between the two countries. Pakistan claimed that India had reached out to it first. The ceasefire froze the conflict, with both sides claiming victory, but it did not stop either from continuing its hostile posturing. 90 Ibid. Prime Minister Modi declared that India would from now on systematically strike back against not just those perpetrating terrorist attacks on Indian soil, but also their backers – a clear allusion to Pakistan. 91 Ibid. These clashes were traumatic for many Indians, particularly in regions which endured missile and drone strikes for the first time. Many Kashmiris experienced it differently, however. Seeing Pakistani drones in their skies, hovering above and firing upon Indian installations in the region, seems to have made an impression on local people. The display of Pakistan’s military capabilities on the first day of the conflict, when it allegedly shot down several Indian fighter jets, likewise had a notable effect on local public opinion. 92 See “Pak’s Fatah 1 rocket debris fished out of Srinagar’s Dal Lake during clean-up”, India Today , 22 September 2025. “The May conflict countered post-2019 hopelessness that Pakistan is not interested in Kashmir”, a Srinagar resident observed. 93 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. B. Weighing the Pakistani Role India insists that Pakistan is responsible for almost all militant attacks in the region, accusing Islamabad of fighting a proxy war in Kashmir, using anti-India jihadist groups such as the Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad. Indian officials also claim that Pakistani fighters are steadily infiltrating Jammu and Kashmir. 94 An Indian security official claimed that there were about 100 foreign (meaning Pakistani) militants in Kashmir. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Concurring with these allegations, a section of Kashmiris also say Pakistan-based jihadist groups, working at Islamabad’s behest, are now spearheading the insurgency in Kashmir. 95 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, 2025. Until recently, Kashmiris had disputed Indian government claims, regarding them as simplistic, albeit without denying Pakistani influence. Instead, they pointed to local young people joining militant ranks out of anger at Indian policies toward the region (see Section III.C). Nowadays, however, many claim that Pakistan is back in the driver’s seat. Establishing the truth regarding these allegations is no easy matter. Pakistan categorically denies India’s claims that it is waging a proxy war in Indian-administered Kashmir. 96 “Pakistan takes ‘strong exception’ to ‘baseless claims’ of Indian army chief”, The News , 15 January 2025. It has repeatedly said it opposes any form of terrorism, and it argues it has clamped down on homegrown jihadist groups blamed for terrorist attacks in India. 97 “Nuclear war ‘wasn’t an option’”, Dawn , 14 May 2025; “FO says Pakistan has ‘dismantled’ terrorist outfits amid U.S. designation of group blamed for Pahalgam attack”, Dawn , 18 July 2025. Lashkar-e-Tayyaba was officially banned in 2002, following an attack on the Indian parliament, as was Jaish-e-Mohammad in 2008 after another in Mumbai. When the groups attempted a comeback under new names, these were also outlawed; Lashkar-e-Tayyaba’s charity front, Jamaat-ud-Dawa, was proscribed in 2008 and Jaish-e-Mohammad’s so-called philanthropic arm, the Falah-i-Insaniyat Foundation, in 2019. The next year, the government froze the properties and assets of both groups. Islamabad also says the leaders and activists of these groups are under house arrest or jailed, including Lashkar-e-Tayyaba chief Hafiz Saeed, whom India now holds responsible for the Pahalgam attack. Convicted of terrorism financing in 2019, Saeed is in prison serving a 33-year sentence. 98 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. The fact that banned anti-India jihadist groups have proven capable of repeatedly re-emerging, only to be outlawed again, tends to undermine Pakistan’s claims that it has eliminated their organisational structures altogether. That said, it does not constitute definitive proof of New Delhi’s allegations that Islamabad is once again waging a proxy war in Jammu and Kashmir, including by sending in jihadist proxies. Pakistani experts say such a policy would undermine the country’s national security and damage its international standing. 99 Crisis Group telephone interviews, Pakistani analysts, August 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in [Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces]. Top Pakistani policymakers reportedly feel that any armed venture could spark conflict with India, leaving the country open to a two-front threat at a time when it confronts a raging insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces, bordering Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, where militant attacks have killed thousands of Pakistan’s security personnel and civilians. 100 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. See also Crisis Group Asia Report N°354, Pakistan: Responding to the Militant Surge on the Afghan Border , 27 February 2026. Islamabad claims that India is backing proxies fighting Pakistan in these regions via its close ties with the Afghan Talban authorities and support for anti-Pakistani insurgents on Afghan soil, namely Baloch militant groups and the jihadist Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (or Pakistani Taliban). 101 Islamabad, however, holds Kabul primarily responsible, alleging that the Afghan Taliban provide safe havens to Pakistani militant groups. “Naqvi holds India responsible for spate of attacks in Balochistan: ISPR says 92 terrorists killed”, Dawn , 31 January 2026; “DGISPR tells Afghan Taliban regime to choose between terrorist organisations and Pakistan”, Dawn , 27 February 2026. Islamabad’s public response has been to highlight Indian human rights violations in Kashmir in international forums, including at the UN Security Council, calling New Delhi out for what it calls “state-sponsored” terrorism against Kashmiri Muslims. 102 “UNSC condemns Swat suicide blast after Pakistan sounds alarm on Afghan terrorist havens”, Dawn , 6 June 2026. In an implied reference to Indian-administered Kashmir, it has also demanded a clear “distinction between terrorism and the legitimate struggle against foreign occupation and the right of self-determination”. 103 “Pakistan calls for internal reform of UN’s counterterrorism architecture”, Dawn , 2 July 2026. Islamabad has gone on to accuse New Delhi of “weaponising” water, warning that it would have no choice but to act, including militarily, should India store or divert waters allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty. 104 The three western rivers allocated to Pakistan under the treaty supply 80 per cent of the country’s total water consumption. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan, Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Despite the rhetoric, the Kashmir dispute appears to have lost much of its prominence in Pakistan as Islamabad’s attention shifts from its South Asian neighbourhood to the Middle East. In September 2025, Pakistan signed a mutual defence agreement with Saudi Arabia, cementing a longstanding partnership; it went on to sign a joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye the following August. Islamabad has also assumed the mantle of mediator since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, leveraging its strategic and diplomatic links with the U.S., as well as its working relationship with neighbouring Iran. 105 Crisis Group Commentary, “Pakistan: A New Player in the Quest for a U.S.-Iran Breakthrough”, 4 June 2026. As a result, Pakistan would appear to have few incentives and little need to meddle in India, let alone support Islamist jihadist proxies in Kashmir, according to one Pakistani analyst. Pakistani policymakers are said to be well aware that backing a proxy war would corroborate the BJP government’s portrayal of Pakistan as a threat to regional stability and global peace. 106 Crisis Group telephone interview, August 2026. Another prominent Pakistani analyst, however, warned that even the “creeping presence” of anti-India jihadist groups, particularly Lashkar-e-Tayyaba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, should be a matter of concern for Islamabad. So long as the authorities do not rigorously enforce the ban on such groups, India’s claims will not ring hollow. 107 Mohammad Amir Rana, “A New Pakistan”, Dawn , 13 July 2025. C. The Delhi Blast and the Threat of Religious Violence On 10 November 2025, a car laden with explosives blew up at a busy intersection in New Delhi, killing fifteen and injuring more than 30 people. 108 “Delhi car blast: Doctors with bombs”, The Hindu , 18 November 2025. The driver, who died in the blast, turned out to be a Kashmiri doctor, seemingly adding a new dimension to conflict in the region. Investigative agencies claim to have uncovered a “white-collar terror” network, including five other physicians from Kashmir; in all, thirteen individuals have been accused of belonging to it so far, including a woman doctor from the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. All Muslim, they were allegedly attempting to revive Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind, an offshoot of al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent. 109 Al-Qaeda’s influence on Kashmiri militancy has been minimal, as Kashmiris consider the group’s ideology too extreme. The presence of a local separatist leadership also reduced the pull of transnational jihadism. Given the Kashmir links, Indian security agencies carried out an extensive crackdown in the Himalayan region, demolishing the suspects’ houses in the process. Despite Prime Minister Modi’s earlier threat to retaliate against Pakistan for every terrorist attack perpetrated in India, the government refrained from immediately blaming Islamabad, possibly out of desire to avoid another war. In the end, the National Investigative Agency concluded the attack was carried out by a group led by medical professionals and inspired by the al-Qaeda splinter rather than Pakistan-backed militants. 110 According to the NIA, the accused formed Ansar Ghazwat-ul-Hind Interim in June 2022, after a failed attempt to travel to Afghanistan, stockpiling arms and ammunition as well as manufacturing explosives using commercially available chemicals. “NIA names three more accused in supplementary chargesheet in Red Fort area blast case”, The Hindu , 27 June 2026. The involvement of physicians in a suicide bombing came as a shock to Kashmiri society. Though militants have carried out suicide attacks in Kashmir in the past and educated individuals have become insurgents, these two trends have rarely overlapped. For now, the attack remains a one-off event, with no evidence that it forms part of a larger trend. That said, it has raised alarm in Kashmir at the prospect that more suicide bomb cells made up of young people may emerge. Though the New Delhi bombers had not previously been jailed, some Kashmiris are concerned that young adults incarcerated under anti-terror laws are being exposed to the influence of hard-core militants and separatist ideologues, and often turn to religion to cope with jail life. 111 Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. Meanwhile, the permanent fear of state surveillance appears to have played a central role in the breakdown of social cohesion and communication in the traditionally close-knit Kashmiri community. 112 “Radicalisation in Kashmir: The ideological transformation”, The New Indian Express , 16 November 2025. “I no longer know how my son thinks or whether he knows about his son”, a former Kashmiri bureaucrat noted, lamenting the fraying of bonds in society. 113 Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, 2025. Investigative agencies claimed that a group of medical professionals from Kashmir was responsible for a suicide blast in New Delhi last November, killing fifteen and injuring many more. Koil, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi Two of the doctors were from Koil village in South Kashmir whose homes were demolished by the security forces. Koli, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi V. A Way Forward It is becoming increasingly clear that India’s efforts to revamp Kashmir by stamping out resistance and establishing central control of its administration have failed. New Delhi should turn the page by recognising the political dispute at the heart of the region’s unrest, eschewing the temptation to view all militancy through a religious lens and reorienting its approach through a series of steps that would allow it to manage the conflict more effectively. A. Restoring Political Rights Though several indicators of unrest in Jammu and Kashmir have steadily declined, including militant violence, street demonstrations and stone throwing, the region is at constant risk of renewed turbulence. Trying to build stability on a foundation of central rule, heavy-handed law enforcement and counter-insurgency is not the right approach. Despite the BJP government’s claims to the contrary, Kashmiri Muslims believe that the changes imposed since 2019 have been motivated by prejudice in the shape of a Hindu nationalist desire to disenfranchise them. As the 2024 elections show, diverse and hitherto antagonistic political forces in Kashmir, from mainstream politicians to separatists, have come together in response to the perceived threat to the region’s community and way of life. Tacit support for militant groups has also grown among a number of Kashmiris, who have come to think that armed struggle is the only way to prevent India from overhauling the region’s socio-religious identity and robbing it of political autonomy. A continued campaign of militant violence, however, is likely to aggravate tensions with New Delhi and fuel bilateral discord between India and Pakistan, stoking instability that is not in the interests of India’s rulers, the Kashmiri people or the rest of South Asia. To avert these risks, it is vital that New Delhi devise an approach to address the wellsprings of public disaffection in the region. New Delhi should first and foremost seek to rebuild a basis of public trust in the region. That should begin with restoration of Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, a step Prime Minister Modi himself has promised to take on several occasions. Though the move would be insufficient to quell all of Kashmiris’ grievances, it would at least remove one source of resentment. Making the chief minister subordinate to the New Delhi appointed lieutenant governor has been widely perceived as a humiliation. Reversing it would, to an extent, help win back Kashmir’s disillusioned pro-India political factions and could help weaken public sympathy for militancy. A decision on the issue nevertheless appears to have been delayed due to the government’s lack of confidence in security conditions following the Pahalgam attack. 114 The head BJP member of Jammu and Kashmir’s legislature said statehood will be restored when the security situation is under control. See “Statehood to J&K only after end to violence against youth, children: BJP’s Sunil Sharma”, PTI, 5 February 2026. More broadly, New Delhi prefers to maintain a firm grip on the region for a couple of reasons: it does not trust regional political forces to tackle militancy, and it seeks to build national political capital by proving it can control violence in Kashmir. Its current approach, however, is self-defeating. In the words of Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, there are “two parallel governments running the same territory”, with the lieutenant governor granted greater powers, especially in matters of public safety. 115 “ The Economic Times : ‘UT with an assembly is the worst form of government’: Omar Abdullah says two govts in J&K can’t work”, video, YouTube, 18 June 2025. Abdullah and other observers note that despite its prerogatives, the administration under the lieutenant governor lacks the grassroots networks needed to track militancy and prevent future attacks. 116 Crisis Group interviews, Srinagar, November 2025. See also “I take full responsibility: J&K LG Manoj Sinha calls Pahalgam attack a security failure”, Times of India , 14 July 2025. Restoring statehood would ... serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. Restoring statehood would also serve New Delhi’s longstanding goal of achieving greater participation by Kashmiris in India’s democracy. For Kashmiris, the image of a disempowered government fosters the perception that voting in elections is futile. The two elections conducted after the change in the region’s status certainly recorded high voter turnout, with even separatists abstaining from their usual boycott calls. Even so, many voters cast their ballots to vent their frustration with New Delhi’s decisions and to keep the BJP at bay, rather than out of conviction that the outcome would make any material change. It was precisely disillusionment with Indian democracy that triggered the first major surge in militant violence in 1989. 117 New Delhi’s rigging of the 1987 regional polls was the trigger for the separatist insurgency that erupted in 1989, with many candidates who had been jailed turning to militancy upon their release. See Praveen Donthi, “ Kashmir Votes to Repudiate Rule from the Centre ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 October 2024. If restoring statehood is not feasible for political or security reasons in the short term, the central government should consider restoring some of the chief minister’s powers in the interim, with a degree of oversight by the lieutenant governor. The chief minister should, at the very least, have the power to appoint civil servants, one of the post’s main functions in all other Indian states and Union territories. The chief minister’s command of the police should also be restored, albeit by increments. Blocking the chief minister’s office from handling the threat of militancy is counterproductive, as security forces working alone cannot properly track local insurgent activity in a complex and evolving conflict. B. Loosening the Iron Grip The government’s determination to claim it has pacified Kashmir places immense pressure on security forces to live up to that expectation, resulting in the widespread use of draconian anti-terror laws against local people suspected of having militant links. But this approach has tended to fuel resentment of the Indian state, even spurring some of those marked for arrest to join or lend support to militant groups. 118 Crisis Group observations, Jammu and Kashmir, 2021-2025. See also “Youth share tales of harassment at PDP meet on why Kashmiri professionals are turning to violence”, The Hindu , 8 December 2025. Measures such as demolishing the homes of suspected militants’ families without investigation increase the collective sense of victimhood. So does dismissing government employees on mere suspicion of ties to insurgents. Given the consequences for those on the receiving end, New Delhi should stop applying its anti-terror laws so broadly. As an official admitted: “It’s better to make an example out of a handful of guilty people than to resort to collective punishment, which will backfire”. 119 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Srinagar, 2024. Kashmiri observers have also voiced growing concern about rising radicalism and religious fundamentalism among the region’s young people, particularly among those arrested under the anti-terror laws who have come to embrace an extremist version of Islam as a way to cope with imprisonment. 120 Kashmiri observers point out that the government’s practice of transferring detained young Kashmiris to prisons outside the region, where most of the inmates are Hindu, is further pushing them to embrace religion. Crisis Group interview, Waheed Ur Rehman Para, member of Legislative Assembly, Srinagar, November 2025. The case of the young Kashmiri doctors who carried out the 2025 New Delhi blast suggests the problem extends beyond those in jail. 121 A Kashmiri legislator said the blast was not just a political act of terror but also had radical religious undertones. Crisis Group interview, Srinagar, November 2025. In private, security officials voice regret that New Delhi is solely focused on eliminating militants, while doing little to create conditions that discourage them or weaken their cause. 122 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Kashmir, 2025. The use of harsh anti-terror laws for minor transgressions such as posts on social media stands out as particularly counterproductive, as does blacklisting young people who have been charged with disturbing law and order when they later apply for government jobs. 123 “J&K cops to deny security clearance to stone pelters for passport, govt jobs”, The Indian Express , 2 August 2021. C. India-Pakistan: Dialogue amid Distrust New Delhi shows little appetite for engagement with Islamabad given the terrorist attacks perpetrated on its territory, for which it has blamed its neighbour. While Islamabad has officially banned the jihadist groups Lashkar-e-Tayyeba and Jaish-e-Mohammad, which are allegedly responsible for many attacks, they have often re-emerged under changed names, including through charity and political fronts. While these too are proscribed, the groups still seem able to revive themselves, prompting New Delhi to accuse Pakistan of failing to take action against them. 124 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. If it is to convince India that its efforts are genuine, Pakistan will need to aggressively enforce its ban on anti-Indian jihadist groups. India, for its part, should rethink its stance that Operation Sindoor has only been paused, as Modi has put it, implying that military action could immediately resume if another terrorist attack occurs. 125 Ibid. While this novel approach is meant to boost India’s deterrence, it puts India on a perpetual war footing and increases the risk of conflict with Pakistan, the consequences of which could be calamitous. 126 Ibid. Kashmiri militants, whether local or foreign, could well aim to conduct another terror attack on Indian soil. 127 The U.S. Directorate of National Intelligence assessed in its 2026 report that “conditions exist for terrorist actors to continue to create catalysts for crises”. See “Annual Threat Assessment of the US Intelligence Community”, Office of the Director of National Intelligence, March 2026, p. 24. For some observers, the next India-Pakistan conflict is thus “a question of when, not if”. 128 “In West Asia, a widening conflict with no clear ends”, Hindustan Times , 7 March 2026; “The faint hope for peace between India and Pakistan”, Time , 26 June 2026. It is true that, despite its combative posture and promises to retaliate against all attacks, the Indian government has proven more cautious than expected, taking great care not to blame Pakistan after the November 2025 New Delhi blast. But whether it can withstand domestic pressure in the event of another large-scale attack is hard to predict. In these circumstances, resuming a modicum of dialogue with Islamabad has taken on extra urgency. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has ... turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. New Delhi has thus far rebuffed Pakistan’s diplomatic overtures, including the Pakistani prime minister’s offer of dialogue to settle contentious issues, from terrorism to disputes over water sharing and the fate of Jammu and Kashmir. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “PM urges India to ‘hold’ meaningful dialogue on Kashmir”, The News , 5 February 2025. Insisting that Pakistan still backs anti-India jihadists, India has also turned down Islamabad’s proposal of back-channel talks. 130 Maleeha Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, Dawn , 15 June 2026. The two sides have reportedly participated in a few discreet Track 1.5 and 2 dialogues, unofficial discussions held by former officials and experts who are not representatives of any state. 131 “India Pakistan held Track 1.5, 2 meetings after Operation Sindoor”, Hindustan Times , 17 April 2026. As a former senior Pakistani diplomat noted, however, such exchanges have limited value since participants seldom deviate from the stated positions of their home countries. 132 Lodhi, “A year on, stalemate persists”, op. cit. Signs of greater inclination to engage with Islamabad have nevertheless begun to emerge on the Indian side. A senior leader from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the BJP’s powerful parent organisation, has for the first time spoken up about the need to engage with Pakistan, arguing that while India has every right to “respond appropriately” to terror incidents backed by Islamabad, it should leave the door to dialogue open. 133 “Why has the RSS called for dialogue with Pakistan?”, The Hindu , 17 May 2026; “‘India should not close doors for dialogue with Pakistan’: RSS general secretary Dattatreya Hosabale”, Times of India , 12 May 2026. Given the RSS’s influence, this stance could help assuage public hostility to diplomacy with Pakistan. 134 The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (the National Volunteers Association, or RSS) is a Hindu nationalist organisation founded in 1925, of which the BJP is just one of many wings. With millions of members, it is considered the largest NGO in the world. For a critical view of the RSS, see “Mamdani opposes NYC event with leader of India’s Hindu nationalist group”, Reuters, 26 August 2026. Islamabad has reacted cautiously to the RSS call, with the foreign ministry waiting to see if its views reflect India’s official policy. 135 “FO waiting to see how India reacts to ‘pro-dialogue chorus”, Dawn , 15 May 2026. Few in Pakistan, however, are optimistic regarding the revival of formal talks with India so long as the BJP government continues to accuse the country of supporting jihadist groups and fighting a proxy war with its neighbour. 136 Crisis Group telephone interviews, August 2026. See also Touqir Hussain, “Modi’s Pakistan policy”, Dawn , 13 August 2026. Hussain is a former Pakistan ambassador. The absence of direct lines of communication beyond military-to-military channels increases conflict risks, including as the result of miscalculation or misunderstanding. Despite abiding distrust of its neighbour, India has, in the past, maintained communication through back channels with Pakistan, even in times of crisis. 137 The prime ministers of India and Pakistan spoke to each other even at the height of the Kargil conflict of 1999, for example, and the two national security advisers have been in regular touch during other tense episodes. At present, however, the only communication channel in place is a hotline between the directors general of military operations. Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. See also “India and Pakistan: Neighbours who do not talk to each other”, The India Forum , 10 April 2026. Since there are few prospects for formal talks between India and Pakistan’s top leaders, behind-the-scenes diplomacy could play a vital role in defusing the threat of fresh clashes. Such quiet contacts could enable political leaders to communicate, if not directly, then at least through their national security advisers. 138 Crisis Group Briefing, India-Pakistan: Avoiding a War in Waiting , op. cit. Reviving such a mechanism would allow both sides to communicate their red lines and, perhaps most importantly, avoid misunderstanding or misinterpretation of the other’s actions. They should establish this bilateral channel outside the limelight to avoid the domestic pressures both might face should news of it leak. At the same time, Indian authorities could make it clear to the public that any level of engagement would not amount to normalising relations or offering concessions to Islamabad, including over its territorial claims on Kashmir. Authorities in Islamabad could also assure the Pakistani public that Pakistan’s position on Kashmir’s disputed status or other contentious issues such as the country’s rights under the Indus Waters Treaty would not be compromised. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both [India and Pakistan] to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Even then, back-channel diplomacy is unlikely to make much headway if the Indian and Pakistani governments succumb to the temptation of nationalist outbursts and tit-for-tat allegations against each other. A tentative diplomatic opening is also likely to fail if Pakistan does not address India’s suspicions of continued support for anti-India jihadist groups more robustly. It is in Islamabad’s interest to rigorously enforce the law banning all jihadist entities. In return, Islamabad will expect New Delhi to respond to its concerns about alleged Indian backing for anti-Pakistan Baloch militant groups and the Pakistani Taliban. Progress in reducing mutual trust on such contentious issues is unlikely to happen overnight. But a high-level back channel between the national security advisers could still play an important role in this respect. Resuming quiet diplomacy would allow both to share, examine and discuss their respective allegations outside the public eye. Foreign governments that enjoy friendly relations with both parties, such as the U.S., the UK, EU member states, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries, can also help stabilise the relationship. Considering India’s sensitivities regarding foreign interference or mediation on the Kashmir issue, external powers should move cautiously with quiet, behind-the-scenes diplomacy. They should emphasise that it is in New Delhi and Islamabad’s mutual interest to ensure a sustainable peace in South Asia, encouraging them to use high-level back channels to defuse potential conflict triggers. After seven years, the tough security measures and federal rule have not only failed to bring peace but may also have fostered support for militant groups in some circles. Srinagar, Kashmir, India. November 2025. CRISIS GROUP / Praveen Donthi VI. Conclusion Seven years after the Indian government revoked Jammu and Kashmir’s special autonomous status, redrew its boundaries, overhauled its administrative set-up and undertook numerous reforms ostensibly to foster peace, the threats to local and regional security from the restive Himalayan region persist – and have arguably grown more serious given their impact on relations with Pakistan. Though the government has succeeded in reducing conflict-related violence, the stringent measures it has employed to do so and the threat it has posed to Kashmiris’ sense of identity are fuelling deep discontent. New Delhi’s efforts to impose central rule appear not to have achieved their goal of eradicating militancy. They may even have fostered support in some circles for insurgent groups. If it is to achieve a durable peace in Jammu and Kashmir, India should address as a priority Kashmiris’ growing disaffection. Ideally, that would start by honouring the promise to restore the region’s statehood, paving the way to reinstatement of a democratically elected regional government with real power. New Delhi should also review its tactics in combating militant groups, particularly by being more discriminating in the way it applies its anti-terror laws. Sparked by a terrorist attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, the brief but intense clashes between India and Pakistan in 2025 were a stark reminder of how devastating this oft-forgotten dispute could be if it gets out of hand. Resumption of some form of dialogue between the two nuclear neighbours is essential, preferably through a discreet back channel. With its aspirations for a “New Kashmir” proving overly optimistic, the Indian government should do more to ensure that this unresolved conflict does not become the trigger for far greater harm. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/23/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 23 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 23 October 2026 CUBA The UN General Assembly will vote next week on its annual resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place for more than six decades. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Michael Bustamante says the confrontation illustrates the unfortunate either-or terms in which the debate is often framed. Decrying the humanitarian consequences of U.S. measures need not mean absolving the Cuban government of responsibility for its economic policy failures or its suppression of dissent. STRAIT OF HORMUZ October has already seen Iran hit more ships in or around the Strait of Hormuz than any previous month of the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February. Tehran’s escalation comes after the volume of crude oil moving through the strait reached pre-war levels, largely through a scheme by which a few risk-tolerant tankers are assuming the danger of hauling barrels through the waterway before transferring their cargo to more risk-averse vessels outside it. Crisis Group expert Chris Newton says the question now is whether Iran can make these “shuttle runs” too costly. If it cannot, it will lose leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. and Gulf Arab countries that may transpire. But if it can, its attacks could prompt retaliatory U.S. strikes. U.S. - UKRAINE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that U.S. intelligence sharing, crucial for advance warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, had been restored. At the same time, there were conflicting reports on a slowdown in Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite system, which it depends on for battlefield communications and defensive drones. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “throttling” of Starlink, which is run by billionaire Elon Musk's company SpaceX, was a technical error that “no one ordered”. The incident nonetheless fuelled speculation that the Trump administration is scaling back intelligence and technological support for Ukraine to strong-arm Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow ahead of the 3 November U.S. midterm elections. Wednesday’s meeting between Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian”, has done the same. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Polls show that a majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding territory in return for a peace settlement. 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case.
